title: Ea-nasir and the oldest complaint letter
hook: Nearly 4,000 years ago, a customer wrote an angry letter about bad copper.
peek: A clay tablet from the city of Ur, written around 1750 BC, is a customer named Nanni complaining to a merchant called Ea-nasir. The copper was poor, his messenger was snubbed, and he wants his money back.
lede: Around 1750 BC, in the Mesopotamian city of Ur, a man named Nanni pressed an angry letter into clay. He had paid a merchant called Ea-nasir for copper ingots and received poor-quality metal. Worse, his messenger had been treated rudely. The tablet survives, and it is often called the oldest known written customer complaint.

bullets.text: Nanni says the copper was not of the grade promised, that his servant was sent back empty-handed through hostile country, and that he will no longer accept anything but good copper. He also asks for a refund.
The tablet was excavated at Ur in the 1920s by the archaeologist Leonard Woolley, in a house thought to belong to Ea-nasir. It has been in the British Museum since 1953.

Ea-nasir traded copper brought by sea from Dilmun, a trading hub usually identified with modern Bahrain. His business is a small window on long-distance trade in the Persian Gulf almost 4,000 years ago.
Nanni was not alone. Several other tablets found in the same house also grumble about Ea-nasir's dealings, which is part of why he became a much-loved internet joke.
